client: I've been having a really hard time since my mom passed away last year from cancer. I can't seem to concentrate at work anymore — I'll sit down to do something simple and my mind just goes blank, or I end up thinking about her and losing an hour without realizing it. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and reaching out — losing your mom, especially to something like cancer, is one of the most profound losses a person can carry, and it makes complete sense that your mind and body are struggling to keep up with everyday life right now. What you're describing, that drifting, the blank moments, the hours lost in memory, those aren't signs that something is wrong with you; they're signs of how deeply you loved her. I'm really glad you're here, and I'd love to understand more about what these past months have been like for you — what does a typical day feel like right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: A typical day feels like I'm moving through fog, honestly. I wake up and for just a second everything feels normal, and then it hits me again that she's gone, and the whole day kind of collapses from there. I end up sitting at my kitchen table for way too long, not eating, not really doing anything, just... existing, I guess.
therapist: That image of waking up and having just that brief moment of normalcy before it all comes rushing back — that sounds absolutely exhausting, like you're losing her again every single morning. The way you described it, "just existing," really stayed with me, and I notice there's a kind of quiet heaviness in how you're carrying all of this, like the weight of it has settled deep. I want to ask gently — in those long moments at the kitchen table, what kinds of thoughts tend to find you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: It's usually just this loop that starts playing, like... did I do enough, was I there enough, did she know how much I loved her. And then it shifts into something uglier, like maybe if I had pushed harder to get her to the doctor sooner, things would have been different. I sit there and I can't stop the what-ifs, even though part of me knows they're not going to change anything.
therapist: What you're describing — that loop of "did I do enough, was I there enough" — is something called complicated grief, and it so often comes with this cruel trick where our minds turn love into evidence against ourselves. I notice that even as you're naming these thoughts, there's a part of you that already knows the what-ifs aren't the truth, and that's actually really important — that part of you is worth listening to. Can I ask, when that loop starts, what does the version of you that *does* know how much you loved her want to say back?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think that part of me... it wants to say that I was there, that I showed up as best I could, but it's so quiet compared to the other voice. It's like the guilt is just so much louder, and it drowns out anything that tries to defend me. I don't know if I trust that quieter voice yet, honestly — it feels almost dangerous to listen to it, like if I let myself off the hook too easily, it means I didn't love her enough.
therapist: What you just said is so profound and worth sitting with — the idea that letting yourself off the hook might mean you loved her less, when actually, the guilt itself *is* the love, just turned inward and weaponized against you. That quieter voice isn't asking you to forget her or love her less; it's asking you to hold the truth that you can have loved her deeply *and* still not have been able to save her — both things can be real at the same time. What do you think it would feel like, even just for a moment, to let that quieter voice speak a little louder?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I think... if I actually let that quieter voice speak, it would feel terrifying, honestly. Like I'd be standing at the edge of something and I'm not sure I wouldn't just fall apart completely. And part of me wonders if I even deserve to feel that kind of relief, you know?
therapist: That fear of falling apart if you let yourself feel relief — I want to gently offer that falling apart isn't the same as being destroyed; sometimes it's actually the beginning of being put back together. And that question of whether you *deserve* relief tells me so much about how hard you've been on yourself through all of this, as though you've appointed yourself the keeper of her memory through your own suffering. What if the relief wasn't about deserving it, but about her — do you think she would want this weight to be the way you carry her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That question just... it hit me somewhere I wasn't expecting. Because no, she wouldn't want this — I know that, I've always known that somewhere deep down, but knowing it and actually believing it feel like completely different things. It's like there's a part of me that thinks if I let go of the pain, I'm letting go of her, and I don't know how to separate those two things.
therapist: What you just named — that pain and her are tangled together in your heart right now — is one of the most common and most tender parts of grief, this fear that healing means leaving them behind. But I want to offer you a different way to see it: the love doesn't live in the pain, it lives in *you*, and it will still be there when the pain softens. What are some of the ways you already carry her that have nothing to do with the guilt — the things that remind you of her that feel warm rather than heavy?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but honestly, it's hard to separate the two right now. When I try to think of warm memories, they almost immediately get swallowed up by this voice that says "but you weren't there enough" or "you should have called more that last month." I guess there are small things, like the way she used to send me recipes even though she knew I never cooked them, and I'd laugh about it with her anyway... but even saying that out loud makes my chest tight.
therapist: That memory of the recipes — her sending them anyway, the two of you laughing about it — that's her, that's *really* her, and I noticed something shift just now as you shared it, like the words were coming quickly but underneath them there was something much quieter and more tender trying to surface. It's okay to slow down for a moment here; you don't have to outrun what that memory brings up. Can you stay with it just a little longer — what do those recipes mean to you now, when you come across them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know, when I come across them now it's like... they're proof that she knew me, you know? Like she took the time to write them out even when I'd said I didn't need them, and now they're just sitting in a folder on my computer and I never open it. I think I'm scared that if I actually look at them properly, I'll have to really feel how much I miss her, and I'm not sure I'm ready for that.
therapist: That folder is holding so much — it's like she's still in there, still knowing you, still sending you something you didn't ask for but that she wanted you to have anyway. The fact that you haven't opened it isn't avoidance in a bad sense; it's you protecting yourself until you feel ready, and there's wisdom in that even if it also feels like being stuck. I'm curious — when you imagine a version of yourself that *was* ready to open it someday, what do you think you'd want to feel in that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think I'd want to feel... not alone, I guess. Like, I'd want someone there with me, or at least to not feel like the walls were closing in after. But even imagining that version of myself, it feels so far away, like I'm describing a stranger.
therapist: The way you said that — "like I'm describing a stranger" — there's something so quietly heartbreaking in that, like grief has made you feel distant from the person you're trying to become, and I want you to know that stranger isn't gone, she's just buried under a lot of pain right now. And what you said about not wanting to be alone — that's not a small thing, that's you knowing exactly what you need, which means some part of you is still looking out for yourself even in the middle of all this. Who in your life, if anyone, feels like someone you could imagine being with in a moment like that?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly... when you ask who I could imagine being with, my mind just kind of goes blank, and that blankness feels worse than anything. There's my sister, I guess, but we've grown so far apart since everything happened, and I don't even know if she'd understand or if she'd just try to fix it and make me feel more alone. It's like the grief has put this glass wall between me and everyone I used to feel close to.
therapist: That image of a glass wall is so vivid and so lonely — being able to see the people you love but not quite being able to reach them, and grief doing that so quietly that you might not even notice it happening until suddenly everyone feels far away. I'm struck by how quickly you spoke just now, like the words were rushing out ahead of something, and underneath them I sense a real exhaustion with carrying this so alone. With your sister — even with the distance between you, I'm curious what it would mean to you if she *could* understand, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
